Olecranon Fractures
 CORE
August 05, 2025
Elizabeth Hubbard, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for olecranon fractures in pediatric
patients.
Perform an appropriate workup for a pediatric patient in whom fracture about the elbow is
suspected.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of olecranon fractures in pediatric patients.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures of the apophysis of the olecranon are relatively uncommon and should increase
suspicion for an underlying condition, such as osteogenesis imperfecta.




Isolated metaphyseal fractures of the olecranon are relatively rare, and surgeons should
rigorously evaluate radiographs for associated injuries, such as fractures of the radial head
and neck, medial epicondyle, coronoid, and lateral condyle.1
Epidemiology
In children, 4% to 6% of fractures occur about the elbow.2
Usually result from a fall on an outstretched hand
Known association between olecranon fractures in pediatric patients and osteogenesis
imperfecta type 13
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The elbow follows a sequential pattern of ossification and fusion (Figure 1; Table 1).

Figure 1 Images show ossification centers. A, Illustration of the distal humerus shows the
mean time of appearance of ossification centers at the distal humerus. B, AP radiograph of a
right elbow demonstrates the different ossification centers. 1 = capitellum, 2 = medial

Hosalkar HS: Medial epicondyle fractures in the pediatric population. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2012;20[4]:223-232.)

Osteology
The olecranon follows a specific pattern of ossification from infancy through
adolescence, ossifying from distal to proximal. Often, two ossification centers are
present within the olecranon apophysis, and these should not be mistaken for a
fracture. If necessary, radiographs of the contralateral elbow may help discern a true
injury from a patient’s normal anatomy1 (Figure 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
3/21

Figure 2 Graphs show simplified skeletal age assessment via the olecranon method
during the accelerating pubertal growth phase of peak height velocity and Risser grade 0
from ages 11 to 13 years in girls and ages 13 to 15 years in boys, with a decelerating
growth phase after elbow fusion. Y cartilage closure = triradiate cartilage closure.
(Reproduced with permission from Charles YP, Diméglio A, Canavese F, Daures JP:
Skeletal age assessment from the olecranon for idiopathic scoliosis at Risser grade 0. J
Bone Joint Surg Am 2007;89[12]:2737-2744.)
Tendons
The triceps tendon attaches to the proximal ulna metaphysis, distal to the physis.
Joints and Ligaments
The annular ligament wraps circumferentially around the radial neck but arises from the radial
side of the ulna. This ligament also is the attachment site for the radial (lateral) collateral
ligaments. The annular ligament and the lateral collateral ligaments stabilize the radiocapitellar
joints and protect against varus stress. The ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) comprises three
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
4/21

bands: the anterior UCL, transverse UCL, and posterior UCL. The ligament complex inserts on the
coronoid process and the medial olecranon. The anterior and posterior bands originate from the
medial epicondyle and resist valgus stress in elbow extension and flexion, respectively.4 The
transverse ligament runs from the olecranon to the coronoid but does not substantially
contribute to joint stability1,5 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustrations of the elbow show the structure of the medial collateral ligament complex
(A) and the lateral collateral ligament complex (B). (Reproduced from Tashjian RZ, Katarincic JA:
Complex elbow instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[5]:278-286.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
A fall onto an outstretched hand with the elbow slightly flexed is the most common
mechanism of injury.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Olecranon fractures generally occur if a child falls onto an outstretched hand; however,
children tend to hyperextend their elbows when they fall, which drives the olecranon
into the olecranon fossa. This typically results in a supracondylar fracture rather than an
olecranon fracture because the olecranon tends to be protected in this position and the
metaphyseal bone of the supracondylar region of the humerus fails in tension.1
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
5/21

Fractures caused by direct impact to the olecranon have been described but are less
common.
Risk Factors
True apophyseal fractures of the olecranon should increase suspicion for an underlying
predisposing condition, such as osteogenesis imperfecta.3,6
Associated Injuries
Associated injuries are common and have been reported in as many as 77% of patients with
an olecranon fracture.1

Associated Injuries
Radial head and neck fractures are most commonly observed in combination with
olecranon fractures; however, other associated fractures include radial shaft and lateral
condyle fractures. Surgeons should not misdiagnose a Monteggia fracture-dislocation or
a Monteggia fracture variant as an isolated olecranon fracture. A careful physical
examination and imaging studies of the radiocapitellar joint may help identify a subtle
Monteggia injury.
Injury Classification
Apophyseal fractures may be the first indication of osteogenesis imperfecta and must be
differentiated from the more common metaphyseal fractures3,6,7 (Figure 4).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
6/21

Figure 4 Lateral radiograph of the elbow of a 10-year-old boy with osteogenesis imperfecta who
presented with elbow pain after a minor fall. (Courtesy of Elizabeth Hubbard, MD, Durham, NC.)
Metaphyseal fractures are classified according to the mechanism of injury.1
Group A: flexion injuries
Group B: extension injuries
Valgus pattern
Varus pattern
Group C: shear injuries
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The provider should obtain a thorough description of events surrounding the injury (Did the
patient fall? Does the patient or family member remember how the patient fell?). Asking about
prior fractures, particularly in patients who present with an apophyseal fracture of the
olecranon, may help determine if the patient may have underlying osteogenesis imperfecta
that has gone undiagnosed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
7/21

Physical Examination
Patients may have swelling and bruising over the olecranon, and, a defect may be appreciated
at the fracture site, particularly if fractures are substantially displaced. Palpation over the
radial head is necessary to rule out a Monteggia fracture. Tenderness over a reduced radial
head indicates a Monteggia fracture with spontaneous reduction of the radial head.
Neurovascular Examination
A thorough neurovascular examination always is indicated; however, neurovascular injury is
not commonly associated with olecranon fractures, particularly in patients with an isolated
injury. Higher energy injuries, particularly if associated with dislocation, may increase the risk
for an associated neurovascular injury.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard AP and lateral radiographs of the elbow are commonly used to diagnose olecranon
fractures.

Radiography
Radiographs should be carefully evaluated for other associated fractures, given the high
frequency with which associated injuries occur. A Monteggia fracture should not
misdiagnosed as an isolated olecranon metaphyseal fracture; therefore, radiocapitellar
alignment should be critically evaluated on all images (Figure 5). If suspicion for an
associated lateral condyle fracture exists, then an internal oblique radiograph should be
obtained because this image is most likely to demonstrate the true degree of fracture
displacement of the lateral condyle fracture.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
8/21

Figure 5 Images of the elbow of an 8-year-old girl who was struck by a car. Lateral (A)
and AP (B) radiographs obtained in the emergency room demonstrate a proximal
olecranon fracture and an anterior radial head dislocation; closed reduction and cast
immobilization were attempted. C, Subsequent lateral radiograph demonstrates
persistent anterior dislocation of the radial head. Intraoperative lateral (D), AP (E), and
lateral (F) fluoroscopic images show open reduction and internal fixation of the
olecranon and closed reduction of the radiocapitellar joint. Postoperative AP (G) and
lateral (H) radiographs demonstrate healing of the olecranon fracture and anatomic
reduction of the radiocapitellar joint.
Computed Tomography
CT is not commonly indicated; however, in patients with a comminuted fracture after
a higher energy injury, CT may aid in preoperative planning.
MRI
MRI is not commonly indicated; however, in patients with normal radiographs, MRI may show
an occult fracture and reveal any associated chondral or ligamentous pathology.8
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
9/21

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Most patients are treated nonsurgically via cast immobilization in relative extension (usually
10° to 45° of flexion) for 3 to 4 weeks. In-cast radiographs are obtained after 7 to 10 days to
ensure alignment remains unchanged.
Greenstick or other nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture patterns are amenable to
nonsurgical management via cast immobilization.
Contraindications
Displaced fractures, particularly those with articular involvement, should be managed
surgically if reduction cannot be achieved or if fracture reduction is not stable in a cast.
Shear-type injuries, especially those with intra-articular extension, are particularly unstable
and should be considered for surgical fixation.
Techniques/Procedures
Immobilization of the elbow in relative extension usually is all that is necessary to maintain
fracture reduction and stability in most patients with an olecranon metaphyseal fracture
(Figure 6).
Figure 6 Lateral radiographs of the elbow of a 7-year-old girl who fell onto her outstretched
hand. A, Radiograph demonstrates a nondisplaced, intra-articular fracture of the right olecranon.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
10/21

B, Repeat radiograph demonstrates immobilization in extension. Radiographs were obtained
weekly in the cast to monitor reduction. Cast immobilization was continued for 4 weeks. C,
Radiograph obtained after cast removal demonstrates healing of the fracture. The patient
regained full flexion, extension, and forearm rotation.
Surgical Management
Indications
Fractures with intra-articular displacement greater than 2 to 3 mm are managed surgically.
Contraindications
Extra-articular fractures that are nondisplaced or minimally displaced and can be reduced and
immobilized in a long arm cast should be managed nonsurgically.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
The fracture pattern often dictates the type of internal fixation that should be used for
olecranon fractures that require surgical management. Careful evaluation of preoperative
imaging studies aids in planning fixation.
Typically, pediatric patients with a simple, noncomminuted fracture can be treated via
Kirschner-wire fixation, a tension-band construct, or lag screw fixation to achieve reduction
and compression across the fracture site.
Older patients and those with a higher mechanism of injury may present with a comminuted
fracture patterns that should be treated via a combination of lag screw and plate fixation, as
the fracture pattern dictates.
Patient Positioning
Patients can be placed in the supine position with the surgical shoulder flexed and adducted
so the forearm rests in pronation on the chest. Alternatively, patients can be placed in the
lateral position with the affected elbow flexed over a radiolucent post.
Surgical Approaches
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
11/21

Usually, a longitudinal incision along the medial border of the olecranon and extending in a
curvilinear fashion proximally around the tip of the olecranon provides direct exposure to the
fracture and preserves a soft-tissue flap directly superficial to the olecranon.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Fixation: stabilized via tension-band fixation, often with the use of an absorbable suture or
sternal wire as the tension band (Figure 7)
Figure 7 Postoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of an elbow demonstrate fixation of a
pediatric olecranon fracture with the use of a tension-band wire construct. (Courtesy of
Elizabeth Hubbard, MD, Durham, NC.)

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Tension-band constructs are the best treatment option for simple, transverse fracture
patterns.9,10 Alternatively, these fractures can be reduced and maintained in reduction
with the use of a single, large cannulated screw over a washer11 or with multiple
compression screws12 (Figure 8). If a single screw is used, then the screw should be
large enough that the threads gain purchase within the inner cortex of the proximal
diaphyseal region of the ulna, and a washer helps distribute the compressive force of the
screw across the proximal olecranon fragment. Oblique, shear fractures can be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
12/21

stabilized with the use of one or two lag screws in older adolescents versus Kirschner
wires in younger patients.2 or with multiple compression screws12 Internal fixation via
lag screws and plate fixation should be considered in patients with more comminuted
fracture patterns (Figure 5).
Figure 8 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) lateral elbow radiographs demonstrate a
displaced olecranon fracture managed with the use of a large cannulated partially
threaded screw and washer to achieve compression at the fracture site. (Courtesy of
Elizabeth Hubbard, MD, Durham, NC.)
In younger patients who potentially are candidates for closed reduction and pinning, an
elbow arthrogram may be useful to assess alignment of the distal humerus, proximal
ulna, and proximal radius after reduction (Figure 9).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
13/21

Figure 9 Images of the elbow of a 4-year-old girl who fell off a slide. Lateral (A) and AP (B)
radiographs demonstrate a left olecranon fracture and a radial neck fracture. The
olecranon fracture was reduced and stabilized with the use of percutaneous Kirschner
wires. Lateral (C) and AP (D) fluoroscopic images show the radial neck fracture, which
was reduced in a closed manner. The patient’s cast and pins were removed 4 weeks
postoperatively. AP (E) and lateral (F) radiographs obtained 10 weeks postoperatively
demonstrate healing of the fractures. The patient regained full elbow flexion, extension,
and forearm rotation.
Postoperative Management
Patients generally are immobilized in a long arm splint or cast for 2 to 3 weeks
postoperatively, after which they are transitioned to a range-of-motion protocol.
The type of internal fixation selected for surgical management of these fractures
should be stable enough to allow for early elbow range of motion to prevent stiffness.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
14/21

Complications
Complications are rare and rarely of clinical importance; however, failure to diagnose
associated injuries (such as radial head dislocation) may result in substantial morbidity.
Hardware Failure
Fixation failure requiring revision open reduction and internal fixation has been reported.
A recent study by Perkins et al9 reported a 14% implant failure rate among patients treated
with the use of tension-band constructs via suture fixation versus a 4% failure rate among
those who were treated with the use of tension-band constructs via wire fixation. Suture-
based tension-band constructs were more likely to fail in older, heavier patients (>50 kg).
Yang et al9 reported that patients treated via compression screws had better functional
outcomes compared with those treated via tension band wiring. Surgical time was decreased
and fewer postoperative complications were observed in the screw cohort compared with the
tension-band cohort.
Stiffness
Slight loss of terminal extension may develop; however, this is not frequently symptomatic or
limiting.1
Patients with an associated elbow dislocation, injury to the distal humerus, and/or injury to the
proximal radius have at greater risk for posttraumatic stiffness12 (Figure 10).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
15/21

Figure 10 Images of the elbow of a 10-year-old girl who sustained an injury on a trampoline. AP
(A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate fractures of the proximal ulna (olecranon and
coronoid) and the radial neck. Intraoperative AP (C) and lateral (D) fluoroscopic images show
open reduction and internal fixation of the olecranon; the radial neck fracture was reduced via
the Metaizeau technique. AP (E) and lateral (F) radiographs obtained after extensive outpatient
physical therapy demonstrate healing of the fractures; however only 10° of forearm pronation
was observed, and the flexion extension arc was from 10° to 140°. G, Subsequent sagittal CT scan
shows proximal radioulnar synostosis.
Other Complications
Patients may report discomfort or tenderness over implants used to manage olecranon
fractures, necessitating a second surgical procedure for implant removal.
In a recent study, 63% of patients underwent implant removal for symptomatic hardware after
surgical management via tension-band constructs.9
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Olecranon Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004069
16/21

Rehabilitation
Early range of motion after a 2- to 3-week period of immobilization for fracture healing is
encouraged to prevent stiffness.
Outcomes
Reported outcomes generally are good, regardless whether patients are treated nonsurgically
or surgically, if no articular displacement is present.
Patients who undergo open reduction and internal fixation should be counseled that the
implants may cause irritation and necessitate removal after fracture healing.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Fractures that are reduced and appear stable and are appropriate for cast management may
lose reduction in the cast. Consideration should be given to monitoring these patients closely
via periodic in-cast radiographs to confirm that the fracture remains reduced in the cast.
Displaced proximal metaphyseal ulna fractures, particularly those with apex radial angulation,
may lead to radial head subluxation, a variant of a Monteggia fracture that occasionally is
missed.
Mark as Complete
